title: Question 2
stem:
The engine of a toy rocket pushes gases vertically downwards and this results in the rocket accelerating vertically upwards from the ground.

The rocket starts to move from rest at time $t = 0$. The variation with time $t$ of the vertical velocity $v$ of the rocket for the first $0.30\,\text{s}$ of the flight is shown in Fig. 2.1.

{{figure:figure_2_1}}

As the rocket moves, the thrust force $T$ provided by the rocket engine is $16\,\text{N}$. Assume that the mass of the rocket is constant for this part of its flight.

Assume that air resistance is negligible.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: For this part of the rocket's flight:
parts.text: show that the acceleration of the rocket is $55\,\text{m s}^{-2}$
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 2.1 and think about what the steepness of that straight line tells you about how quickly velocity is changing, and pick two easy points on the line to read off the overall change.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link the Graph Shape to Motion**
A straight line on a velocity-time graph means velocity is increasing at a steady rate. That steady rate of change of velocity is the acceleration, so you can find it from the steepness of the line.

Step 2: **Read Off the Change and Calculate**
From rest at $t = 0$, the velocity reaches about $v = 16.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 0.30\text{ s}$. So $$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{16.5 - 0}{0.30 - 0} = 55\text{ m s}^{-2}$$ This confirms the stated value.

key_concepts: gradient of velocity-time graph equals acceleration
uniform acceleration from straight-line v-t graph

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: state an expression for the resultant force $F$ experienced by the rocket in terms of the thrust force $T$ and the weight $W$ of the rocket
hints: Hint 1: Picture the two vertical forces on the rocket and think about which one points up and which one points down to decide how they combine to give the net upward push.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sort Out the Directions**
Thrust $T$ pushes the rocket up while weight $W = mg$ always pulls down toward the Earth. Resultant force means what is left over after they oppose each other.

Step 2: **Write the Net Upward Force**
Taking upwards as positive: $$F = T - W$$ That is the unbalanced force that actually accelerates the rocket upwards.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: calculate the mass of the rocket.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the law that connects the resultant force you just wrote down to the mass and the acceleration you found from the graph.
Hint 2: Replace $F$ and $W$ with $ma$ and $mg$, then rearrange to make $m$ the subject using $T = 16\text{ N}$, $a = 55\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Combine Newton's Second Law with Weight**
The net force causes the acceleration: $F = ma$. Putting in your expression for $F$ gives $$ma = T - mg$$ A common slip is to forget weight and just use $T = ma$. The engine must both lift the weight and accelerate the rocket.

Step 2: **Solve for the Mass**
Factor $m$ and rearrange before putting numbers in: $$m(a+g) = T$$ $$m = \frac{T}{a+g} = \frac{16}{55 + 9.81}$$ $$m = 0.25\text{ kg}$$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
At time $t = 0.30\,\text{s}$, a small piece of metal separates from the rocket.

Calculate:
parts.text: the height of the rocket above the ground at $t = 0.30\,\text{s}$
hints: Hint 1: Remember what the total area between the line in Fig. 2.1 and the time axis represents for the motion from $t = 0$ to $t = 0.30\text{ s}$.
Hint 2: Use the shape you see - a triangle starting from the origin - with base $0.30\text{ s}$ and height $16.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to work out that area.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See Distance as Area**
Velocity multiplied by time gives distance, so adding up lots of little $v \times \Delta t$ strips means the height risen is the area under the $v$-$t$ graph. Here it is a simple triangle from rest.

Step 2: **Calculate the Triangular Area**
$$s = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.30 \times 16.5$$ $$s = 2.5\text{ m}$$ This is the same as using $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ with $u = 0$ and $a = 55\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

enrichment.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: area under v-t graph equals displacement
hints: Hint 1: Remember what the total area between the line in Fig. 2.1 and the time axis represents for the motion from $t = 0$ to $t = 0.30\text{ s}$.
Hint 2: Use the shape you see - a triangle starting from the origin - with base $0.30\text{ s}$ and height $16.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to work out that area.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: the speed at which the piece of metal strikes the ground.
hints: Hint 1: Think carefully about how fast and in which direction the small piece of metal is moving at the exact instant it breaks away at $t = 0.30\text{ s}$.
Hint 2: Once it is free, the thrust no longer acts on it, so identify the only acceleration it feels on the way down and the distance it must fall back to the ground.
Hint 3: Choose the SUVAT equation that links the starting speed, the acceleration over distance $s$, and the final speed without needing time.
parts.proper_answer: $u = 16.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ upwards, $v^2 = u^2 + 2gs$ with $s = 2.5\text{ m}$ gives $v = 18\text{ m s}^{-1}$ downwards.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Get the Starting Conditions for the Fall**
At separation the metal is not starting from rest. It keeps the rocket's velocity, so $u = 16.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ upwards from a height $s = 2.5\text{ m}$. It will first keep rising a little, then fall.

Step 2: **Apply Free-Fall Acceleration**
After separation the only force (air resistance negligible) is weight, so acceleration is $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$ downwards. For speed at the ground we can treat the whole drop with: $$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$ where $a = g$ and $s$ is the height fallen.

Step 3: **Calculate the Impact Speed**
$$v^2 = 16.5^2 + 2 \times 9.81 \times 2.5$$ $$v^2 = 272.25 + 49.05 = 321.3$$ $$v = 18\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ to 2 s.f. This is the speed (magnitude) on striking the ground.
